content: Education and training interventions alone are rarely evaluated in relation to surgical site infection (SSI) rates. Typically, these interventions are combined with specific technical changes to improve outcomes. Examples of improvement interventions for reducing SSIs include implementing automatic stop orders to prevent prolonged surgical antibiotic prophylaxis (SAP) after procedures, transitioning from paper wraps to metal containers for surgical instruments, and establishing pre-approval policies for rapid processing in sterile departments. Engaging attending surgeons to directly observe and confirm improved skin preparation techniques, as well as pre-surgery patient reminders for bowel preparation and preoperative bathing, are also effective strategies. Key elements for successful execution include clear protocols, standardized care bundles, and checklists aimed at frontline staff to streamline evidence-based practices. Safety and quality improvement models facilitate stepwise implementation and rapid identification of inefficiencies. This process often involves direct observation by senior clinicians, combined chart audits, and targeted monitoring tools, such as surgical checklists and environmental cleaning algorithms. Sharing evaluation results fosters education and engagement among multidisciplinary teams, increasing awareness and addressing gaps in care processes. Personalized feedback to clinicians and external reviews of implementation processes also contribute to improvement. Barriers to success include relying on single interventions, lack of leadership involvement, insufficient resources, and poor communication. Addressing these barriers early in the implementation process is critical. This program, implemented in several African countries, highlighted the importance of local leadership, multidisciplinary teamwork, and data-driven decision-making. The WHO multimodal strategy for SSI prevention builds on proven models, such as the hand hygiene improvement strategy, and incorporates system changes, education, monitoring, and feedback. By addressing local needs and prioritizing actions, this strategy aims to reduce SSI rates and improve patient outcomes.
